title: Course Schedule
notes:
Task and constraints: Decide whether all numCourses can be completed from prerequisite edges, with b required before a.
Idea: Build graph[prereq] lists and indegree counts, enqueue every zero-indegree course, then pop courses and decrement each neighbor's indegree; count completed nodes.
Technique and why it applies: Kahn's topological-sort algorithm removes available courses and detects cycles by whether all vertices can be removed.
Invariant: Queue entries have no unmet prerequisites, and indegree records remaining incoming edges.
Edge cases: No prerequisites queues every course; [[1,0]] permits two courses; a cycle leaves completed below numCourses.
Complexity: Time O(V+E), space O(V+E).
complexity_reason: The graph stores V vertices and E prerequisite edges, each processed once.

title: Course Schedule
notes:
Task and constraints: Return whether a directed prerequisite graph over numCourses vertices is acyclic.
Idea: Build adjacency lists and indegree, queue all zero-indegree courses, remove each node, decrement its neighbors, and enqueue neighbors when their indegree reaches zero.
Technique and why it applies: Kahn's topological sort completes exactly the vertices that can be ordered without violating prerequisites.
Invariant: Every queued node has no remaining incoming edge from an unprocessed course.
Edge cases: An empty edge list completes all courses; a simple prerequisite chain succeeds; a directed cycle prevents completed from reaching numCourses. ArrayDeque only stores non-null integers.
Complexity: Time O(V+E), space O(V+E).
complexity_reason: Each vertex is queued once and each prerequisite edge decrements one indegree.

title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
notes:
Task and constraints: Support insert, exact search, and prefix search for lowercase words using a trie.
Idea: Each Trie node has children and terminal; insert creates missing child nodes and marks the final node, while search checks terminal and startsWith only checks path existence.
Technique and why it applies: A character trie shares common prefixes and supports operations proportional to query length.
Invariant: node always represents the prefix consumed so far, and terminal distinguishes a stored word from a prefix only.
Edge cases: Searching an inserted word succeeds; a prefix of that word succeeds in startsWith but may fail search; empty word marks the root terminal.
Complexity: O(L) per operation; space O(total inserted characters).
complexity_reason: Each operation follows one child per character and new nodes are created only for missing edges.

title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
notes:
Task and constraints: Implement lowercase Trie insertion, exact search, and prefix checks.
Idea: Node has 26 children and terminal; insert indexes children by ch-'a', and search/startsWith use walk to follow each character or return null on a missing link.
Technique and why it applies: A fixed-alphabet trie shares prefixes and makes each operation depend on word length.
Invariant: walk returns the node for the entire text only when every character edge exists; terminal then distinguishes full words.
Edge cases: Inserted words are found; a stored prefix may pass startsWith but fail search; empty text returns root from walk. Non-lowercase input would produce invalid array indices outside the contract.
Complexity: O(L) per operation; space O(total inserted characters).
complexity_reason: walk examines each character once, and each new trie node owns a fixed 26-slot array.

title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the shortest contiguous subarray with sum at least target, returning zero if none exists; nums are positive.
Idea: Expand right while adding value to total, then while total meets target update best, subtract nums[left], and advance left.
Technique and why it applies: Positivity makes the window sum monotonic under expansion and ensures shrinking can find the shortest qualifying window ending at right.
Invariant: total equals the sum of nums[left:right+1] after each expansion and shrink.
Edge cases: The sample returns 2 for [4,3]; no qualifying sum returns 0; positive values are essential for this shrinking logic.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: right and left each advance at most n times, and only scalar window state is stored.

title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the minimum length of a contiguous subarray summing to at least target, or zero if absent.
Idea: Add nums[right] to long sum; while sum>=target update best and remove nums[left] as left advances.
Technique and why it applies: A sliding window works because all elements are positive, so moving left reduces sum and moving right increases it.
Invariant: sum matches the current window, and best is the shortest qualifying window encountered so far.
Edge cases: The example has minimum length 2; an impossible target returns 0; long sum protects against accumulation overflow from many positive int values.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: Both bounds move only forward through nums and the method stores a constant number of variables.

title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
notes:
Task and constraints: Store words and search patterns where '.' matches any one lowercase letter.
Idea: addWord follows or creates nested dictionaries and marks terminal with '#'; search recursively visits the matching child or tries every nonterminal child for a dot.
Technique and why it applies: Trie DFS shares prefixes, while wildcard branching explores each possible letter at that position.
Invariant: visit(node,index) is true exactly when the suffix word[index:] can finish a stored word below node.
Edge cases: Adding 'bad' makes search('bad') true; 'b.d' explores children at the middle; empty word is represented by '#' at root. '#' is reserved as terminal marker.
Complexity: Add O(L), search O(26^L) worst case; space O(total inserted characters).
time_complexity: Add O(L); search O(26^L) worst case
complexity_reason: addWord creates one dictionary edge per new character and wildcard DFS may branch across 26 children per position.

title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
notes:
Task and constraints: Implement WordDictionary with addWord and wildcard search, where each dot represents one lowercase character.
Idea: addWord creates missing Node children; search calls dfs(root,word,0), which checks terminal at end, explores every existing child for '.', or follows the indexed letter child.
Technique and why it applies: Trie paths handle literal characters directly and DFS branches only at wildcard positions.
Invariant: dfs(node,index) answers whether the remaining suffix can reach a terminal node from this prefix.
Edge cases: A stored word matches exactly; 'b.d' tests child branches at the dot; an empty word checks root. Java recursion depth follows pattern length and can exhaust stack for extreme inputs.
Complexity: Add O(L), search O(26^L) worst case; space O(total inserted characters).
time_complexity: Add O(L); search O(26^L) worst case
complexity_reason: Insertion touches each character once; wildcard DFS can explore up to 26 choices at each position.

title: House Robber II
notes:
Task and constraints: Maximize nonadjacent house values arranged in a circle, where first and last are adjacent.
Idea: Return nums[0] for one house; otherwise linear(values) uses prev2 and prev1 recurrence, and rob takes the maximum for nums without the last versus nums without the first.
Technique and why it applies: Excluding one endpoint in each linear DP case ensures the circularly adjacent endpoints are never both selected.
Invariant: prev1 is the optimum for the processed prefix and prev2 for the prefix before its last house.
Edge cases: [2,3,2] returns 3; one house returns its value; empty nums is not handled and the code assumes at least one house.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1) auxiliary.
complexity_reason: linear scans each of the two slices once and keeps two DP totals.

title: House Robber II
notes:
Task and constraints: Rob a circular row of houses without choosing adjacent houses, including the wraparound pair.
Idea: Handle one house directly; otherwise compare linear(nums,0,n-1) with linear(nums,1,n), where each helper uses prev2/prev1 recurrence.
Technique and why it applies: The two ranges represent all solutions excluding the last or excluding the first house, respectively.
Invariant: In linear, prev1 is best for the processed range prefix and prev2 is best before its final element.
Edge cases: [2,3,2] returns 3; a singleton returns nums[0]; empty input would index incorrectly at nums[0] and is outside the expected constraints.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The two linear calls together scan at most 2n elements and each uses two integer states.

title: Contains Duplicate
notes:
Task and constraints: Detect whether any integer appears more than once in nums.
Idea: Build set(nums) and compare its size with len(nums); a smaller set means at least one duplicate was removed.
Technique and why it applies: Set uniqueness compresses repeated values, making cardinality a duplicate test without pairwise comparisons.
Invariant: The set contains exactly the distinct values encountered in the input.
Edge cases: [1,2,3,1] returns true; an empty list returns false; all-distinct values produce equal lengths.
Complexity: Expected O(n) time, O(n) space.
complexity_reason: Constructing the set processes all n values and stores at most n distinct values.

title: Contains Duplicate
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true when an int array contains a duplicate.
Idea: Add each value to seen; if add returns false, the value was already present and the method returns true, otherwise finish with false.
Technique and why it applies: HashSet insertion reports whether a new distinct element was added, allowing early exit on the first repeat.
Invariant: seen contains all values from the processed prefix, without duplicates.
Edge cases: [1,2,3,1] returns true on the last element; an empty array returns false; a singleton returns false. Hash collisions are handled by the set's equality checks.
Complexity: Expected O(n) time, O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The loop inserts each value at most once into seen and may stop at the first duplicate.

title: Contains Duplicate II
notes:
Task and constraints: Find equal values at indices no farther than k apart.
Idea: For each index i and value, check last for a prior index; return true when i-last[value]<=k, then update last[value]=i.
Technique and why it applies: A last-seen map reduces each value's history to its most recent occurrence, which is the closest earlier match.
Invariant: last[value] is the latest index of that value in the processed prefix.
Edge cases: [1,2,3,1], k=3 returns true; k=0 cannot match distinct indices; repeated values farther apart than k do not trigger success.
Complexity: Expected O(n) time, O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The loop performs one map lookup and update per index and stores at most n keys.

title: Contains Duplicate II
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether duplicate values occur within distance k in an array.
Idea: last.put(nums[i],i) returns the previous index; if it exists and i-previous<=k, return true.
Technique and why it applies: HashMap stores the most recent index, and comparing it finds the closest earlier duplicate.
Invariant: After each iteration, last maps every processed value to its latest index.
Edge cases: The sample returns true for k=3; k=0 never accepts two different indices; a duplicate outside the window is overwritten with the current index. Java subtraction follows int arithmetic under normal index bounds.
Complexity: Expected O(n) time, O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The loop makes one put operation per array item and stores one entry per distinct value.

title: Invert Binary Tree
notes:
Task and constraints: Invert every node's left and right children and return the same tree's root.
Idea: Return None at a null node; otherwise recursively invert the old right subtree into left and old left subtree into right using tuple assignment, then return root.
Technique and why it applies: Recursive postorder-style inversion applies the same child swap to every subtree.
Invariant: After each call returns, the node's descendants have already been inverted and its children are exchanged.
Edge cases: Null root returns None; a leaf is unchanged; the sample root's children 2 and 7 exchange sides. Recursion depth can reach tree height h.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(h) recursion.
complexity_reason: The recursion visits each node once and stores one stack frame per tree level.

title: Invert Binary Tree
notes:
Task and constraints: Mirror a binary tree by swapping left and right children at every node.
Idea: Return null for null root, save oldLeft, assign root.left from the inverted right subtree and root.right from inverted oldLeft, then return root.
Technique and why it applies: Recursive subtree inversion mirrors every descendant while preserving the original node objects.
Invariant: On return, both child subtrees have been inverted and attached to opposite sides.
Edge cases: Null stays null; a leaf is unchanged; [4,2,7,1,3,6,9] becomes [4,7,2,9,6,3,1]. Java uses oldLeft to avoid losing that reference before the first assignment.
Complexity: Time O(n), space O(h) recursion stack.
complexity_reason: Each node is visited once, and recursive frames are proportional to the tree height.

title: Summary Ranges
notes:
Task and constraints: Compress sorted unique integers into consecutive ranges, using a singleton string when a run has one value.
Idea: At index i save start, advance while the next value is current+1, append either start or start->nums[i], then move past the run.
Technique and why it applies: Boundary scanning groups consecutive values without building intermediate ranges for every element.
Invariant: Before each outer iteration, all indices below i belong to already emitted runs.
Edge cases: Empty input returns []; [7] emits '7'; [0,1,2,4,5,7] emits three ranges. The code assumes sorted unique input as stated.
Complexity: Time O(n), O(1) auxiliary space excluding output.
complexity_reason: The inner and outer loops advance i monotonically so each number is examined a constant number of times.

title: Summary Ranges
notes:
Task and constraints: Summarize consecutive runs in a sorted unique int array as ranges or singleton strings.
Idea: Save nums[i] as start, advance while nums[i+1]==nums[i]+1, append a singleton or start->end, and continue at the next run.
Technique and why it applies: Run-boundary detection emits one output per maximal consecutive segment.
Invariant: Every index before i has been included in exactly one emitted range.
Edge cases: Empty input yields an empty list; [7] yields "7"; the sample yields "0->2", "4->5", "7". The condition checks i+1 against length before indexing it.
Complexity: Time O(n), auxiliary space O(1) excluding output.
complexity_reason: The index only moves forward across the array and result stores one string per run.

title: Power of Two
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether n is a positive power of two.
Idea: Require n>0 and test whether n & (n-1) equals zero.
Technique and why it applies: A positive power of two has exactly one set bit; subtracting one clears it and sets all lower bits, so the AND is zero.
Invariant: The expression tests the bit pattern directly without iterating through candidate powers.
Edge cases: 16 returns true; 3 returns false; zero and negative numbers fail the positivity check.
Complexity: Time O(1), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The method evaluates a positivity check and one bitwise expression.

title: Power of Two
notes:
Task and constraints: Return whether a signed int is a positive power of two.
Idea: Check n>0 and then test (n & (n-1))==0.
Technique and why it applies: For a positive power of two, the single set bit is cleared by subtracting one; every other positive number leaves a shared set bit.
Invariant: The boolean expression accepts only positive values with one set bit.
Edge cases: 16 returns true; 3 returns false; zero and negative ints fail n>0 before the bit test. Java int subtraction follows fixed-width arithmetic, but positivity excludes the problematic nonpositive cases.
Complexity: Time O(1), space O(1).
complexity_reason: The method performs two constant-time integer checks and stores no extra data.
